content:
Bloomberg reported that the UK plans to legislate to require Apple and Google to "prevent children from using mobile phones and tablets to capture, share, or view nude images." Details below.

Apple said it plans to strengthen its "Communication Safety" feature

Speaking to Parliament today, UK Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said the government plans to introduce new legislation requiring major tech platforms, including Apple and Google, to establish "device-level protections" to prevent children from "using their devices to capture, share, or view nude images."

She noted that the relevant bill would be submitted to Parliament for review "as soon as possible." Previously, in June, the government had given tech companies a three-month deadline to voluntarily introduce such protections.

Delivering a speech in the House of Commons, Nandy acknowledged that Apple and Google have since made "meaningful changes," but she also pointed out that these changes "have not matched the scale of this crisis."

Excerpts from her statement are as follows:

Children face an unacceptable level of sexual harm online. They are lured, coerced, and manipulated into producing and sharing intimate images across various online services. The Internet Watch Foundation believes that 91% of these images are self-produced by children. These images are used for extortion and sexual blackmail. Each year, approximately 9,000 child sexual abuse cases involve an online element, and minors account for nearly a quarter of online blackmail cases.

Nandy added that device-level protections are only one of two measures the government plans to implement; the second is requiring apps used by children to "prevent them from accessing or sharing nude content."

In a statement to Bloomberg, Apple said the company "shares the UK's commitment to combating online exploitation and abuse, and has shared with UK officials its plans to further strengthen the 'Communication Safety' feature and other tools to help protect children."

Apple also noted that it launched "a feature in 2021 that prevents children from viewing or sharing photos or videos containing nudity," and added that "this feature now supports third-party apps."
